prompt: The Shipper team asks Renata, who owns the import standard, for an exception: its invoice screen would import a module inside Payments' package to show whether the driver has been paid. Payments' `api.py` already offers a function that answers exactly that, which the team had not found. Renata refuses. Which reply refuses the way both courses ask?
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 9; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 8.

choices.text: No. The import rule is a must, and a must has no unless. Please read the nine standards again, with their reasons, before you file another request.
choices.why: It says no clearly and stops there: no sign the need was heard, no alternative, and a lecture where a reason in the asker's unit belonged.

choices.text: You want shippers to see that a payout went through. Not via Payments' internals: a change there breaks your page silently. Its `api.py` covers it; if a field is missing, ask with a date and owner.
choices.why: The need said back, a plain no, the reason in their terms, a real alternative and what would change the answer. Carreto's refusals came with a cheaper way to meet the standard, like this one.

choices.text: Unfortunately I'm afraid an exception might be difficult just now, with everything else on the list, but I will try to fit it in once the quarterly review is out of the way.
choices.why: Softening words make a no unclear, and an unclear no is heard as a yes; "I will try" is a promise with no date behind it.

choices.text: Granted until Payments has time to extend its `api.py` with whatever your invoice screen needs; I will add the entry to the list inside the check today, so that your build stays green in the meantime.
choices.why: "When the other team has time" is not a date, and the function the screen needs already exists, so there is nothing to excuse.

prompt: For the third time this quarter, Matching and Tracking argue in a channel over a change to a table that both of them write, and each time the change is settled by whoever happens to be online. Both tech leads ask Renata to mediate. What do the two courses have her do?
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 16; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 9.

choices.text: Settle each change on its merits as it comes up, because a mediator's job is the argument in front of her and not the org chart
choices.why: Arguments between teams recur because something shared has no owner; settling each one leaves every next change a fresh negotiation.

choices.text: Take ownership of the table herself, so that every later change has a single neutral person who must approve it first
choices.why: A mediator who decides becomes the next owner of the shared thing, and every future argument about it then lands on her desk.

choices.text: Give the table to whichever team writes the most rows to it, and let the other team read a copy kept in step
choices.why: Volume is not the test: the owner is the team whose service would suffer most from a bad change to it.

choices.text: Get the table one owning team and a written contract, decided as who owns which data, with both leads asked first
choices.why: Who owns which data is the architect's row of the decision-rights table, after asking the tech leads; the owner and its contract are what stop the next fight, and she stays out of owning it.

prompt: One risk in the instant-payout register has been priced as an exposure per quarter, and the only reduction anybody has found would cost more each quarter than that exposure. Renata is writing the page for Sílvio, who owns the money. What do the two courses have her put on it?
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 14; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 4.

choices.text: Each response with what it costs, acceptance among them, and the choice left to the budget owner
choices.why: Accepting is a correct choice when reducing costs more than the risk is worth, and only the budget owner makes it; if he does, the register records who, a review date and a trigger.

choices.text: Nothing: a risk whose fix costs more than the risk itself is accepted already and needs no line on a director's page
choices.why: That is accepting by default, because nobody decided; an acceptance counts only when the person who owns the budget makes it and it is written down.

choices.text: The risk marked critical, so that the reduction gets its funding before the exposure has a chance to grow
choices.why: Escalating a small risk as critical trains directors to discount every alarm, the real one included.

choices.text: The reduction as already chosen, because the architect owns the technical risks and so picks the response to each
choices.why: Making the consequences explicit is the architect's work; choosing among them belongs to the people who own the money and the product.

prompt: Paula wants a rule that every event a service publishes carries a schema version, which every team would have to follow. Her draft is a long decision record holding her research notes and every option argued in full, opened as a pull request that the tech leads may comment on whenever they like. What do the two courses suggest?
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 5; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 2.

choices.text: Keep it as the record: a decision record has to hold the whole argument, or a reader two years on cannot follow why it was decided
choices.why: A record that grows into a design document stops being read; the long argument belongs in a proposal, and the record is the page left after it.

choices.text: Send a one-pager to Tomás instead, since a rule for every team is one change approved by one person
choices.why: A one-pager suits a change one known person approves; a rule other teams must follow needs the people it affects to comment.

choices.text: Argue it as an RFC with a closing date and a named decider, then keep a short record of the decision, its reason and its cost
choices.why: A rule other teams must follow is what an RFC is for, and the record is what remains once it is decided: what, why and what it costs.

choices.text: Split the draft into several smaller records, one per option considered, each carrying a status line of its own
choices.why: A record is one decision; the options that lost belong inside its context, not in records of their own.

prompt: Renata recommended putting the payout provider behind an interface Payments owns before going live. Helena and Sílvio choose to call the provider directly and go live a week sooner: a legitimate trade, breaking no constraint. What do both courses expect of her next?
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 13; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 7.

choices.text: Record only the chosen option in the decision record, so that the log does not show the directors divided
choices.why: The options that lost and her recommendation stay in the record, so a reader later can see the trade was made knowingly.

choices.text: Record the decision as taken, with her recommendation and its reason; enter the debt; help build what they chose
choices.why: Losing a recommendation is part of the job: the record keeps what was recommended and why, the debt gets its entry, and she helps make the chosen option work.

choices.text: Decline to sign the record, because skipping the interface is a constraint the business may not choose
choices.why: Only something like an illegal or unsafe plan is outside the business's choice; this one trades future cost for speed.

choices.text: Agree in the room, then raise the interface again at each planning meeting until the decision is reopened
choices.why: A quiet campaign at every planning meeting is relitigating; the decision is reopened when new evidence arrives, not by repetition.

prompt: Renata asks Tomás for three weeks across Pricing, Payments and Platform to remove four services. Which belong in her request? Choose all that apply.
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 12; Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 4.

choices.text: The upgrade hours and the pages that each service raises, beside its row of the inventory
choices.why: The cost of keeping a service has no bill attached; putting hours and pages beside each row is what made Tomás see it.

choices.text: That the four are fragile technical debt, and that the platform will not scale unless they go
choices.why: Adjectives lose to requests that arrive with a number; "fragile" describes the system, and the decision is about time and money.

choices.text: That Pricing pays about two weeks of the work while the saving lands on Platform and on-call
choices.why: Cost on one team and saving spread across all is why no team's roadmap carries removal, and why the architect asks.

choices.text: How geo-distance's routing library would run in-process, so Tomás can check the merge himself
choices.why: Tomás decides whether three weeks are worth it; how the library moves is method, for the team that does the work.

prompt: Bruno's cap on instant payouts for new drivers lowers the judged loss from a fraud ring from R$ 180,000 to about R$ 45,000, with the chance of one in a quarter still judged at 20%. By how many reais a year does the cap lower the exposure?
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 14.

prompt: Pricing needs to know which drivers are online. Matching's cache already holds that list, Pricing's service can reach the cache today, and reading it directly would work on the first afternoon. In Hickey's terms, where does that choice sit?
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 12.

choices.text: Simple and easy: one read, no new service and nothing extra to deploy
choices.why: Fewer boxes is not simple; the read ties Pricing to the inside of Matching, which is exactly what simple means not doing.

choices.text: Hard and simple: an unfamiliar path, though it keeps the two teams apart
choices.why: The path is the familiar one, already in reach, and it joins the teams rather than keeping them apart.

choices.text: Hard and complex: both teams must coordinate before anything works
choices.why: Nothing needs coordinating on the first afternoon; the coupling shows later, the first time Matching changes its cache.

choices.text: Easy and complex: close at hand, and it braids two teams together
choices.why: Easy is what is near at hand; complex is what is braided together. Like Payments reading Tracking's table, it is the trap corner.

prompt: Sílvio wants to read Carreto's container diagram, and he never opens a repository. Paula offers to copy the diagram onto a page of the finance wiki once a quarter. What does Carreto do instead?
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 8.

choices.text: The pipeline publishes `docs/` to the internal site on each merge, dated and linked back; nobody edits that copy
choices.why: The source lives in one place and is published to wherever its readers are; the copy is regenerated, so it cannot drift.

choices.text: Paula's quarterly copy, as long as the wiki page carries an owner, and the date it was last checked, written at its top
choices.why: An owner and a date stop a page being trusted by mistake, but a hand copy still lives away from every change to the system.

choices.text: A hand-drawn diagram kept on the finance wiki just for him, because docs as code is a practice meant for engineers
choices.why: Readers outside engineering are served by publishing from the repository, not by a second source that nothing keeps true.

choices.text: Read access to the repository for Sílvio, so that he can read the one source directly
choices.why: He should not have to open repositories; the answer is to take the source to him, rendered.

prompt: The Driver app could ask for a fresh login before every change to a driver's payout details: safer if a phone is stolen, irritating every time. Put Renata's habit with a trade-off point like this one in order.
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 6.
items: Write a security scenario and a usability scenario, each with a response measure
Name the person who owns each of the two sides
Put the options in front of those owners, saying what each costs which side
Write down what was chosen as a decision record, with the scenarios in its context
trap: Going to the owners first is tempting, but without scenarios that carry a response measure each side arrives with an adjective, and an adjective cannot be traded.

prompt: Services that talk through each other's tables, three ways of publishing an event and nobody able to say who owns a table: Brian Foote and Joseph Yoder called the result a big ball of ___.
hint: The Role of the Software Architect, lesson 17.

prompt: Explaining the Friday checkout failures to Caio, an engineer says checkout and the route planner are "two families sharing one small kitchen at dinner time". Caio answers: "Then let's pay for a bigger kitchen." What went wrong, by the lesson?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 3.

choices.text: Nothing went wrong: an analogy works when the reader extends it, and Caio has reached a fix on his own
choices.why: He reached the larger server, which only moves the limit; the analogy carried him to the option the proposal rejected.

choices.text: The image was too homely for a finance director, and a more technical one would have kept him from guessing
choices.why: The image did its job for the first point; the trouble is what he did with the part of it that does not hold.

choices.text: He reasoned from the part where it breaks; use it for one point, then say where it stops holding
choices.why: Every analogy breaks somewhere and the reader reasons from the broken part; a good one is used once and its limit stated.

choices.text: Analogies are jargon in disguise; the message should have given Caio the connection limit as a number
choices.why: An analogy lets a reader borrow intuition; the lesson keeps it and asks for its limit, not for a configuration figure.

prompt: Near the end of her ten minutes, Caio asks Lívia what the replica will cost in its third year, a figure she has not worked out. What is the better answer, by the lesson?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 5.

choices.text: A round figure on the spot, since a decider expects the person presenting to know her own numbers by heart
choices.why: A guess that turns out wrong discredits everything else she said, the parts she had worked out included.

choices.text: Turn it back to him, and ask Caio which figure for the third year he would be willing to accept
choices.why: That answers a question with a question to the person deciding; he asked for a fact, and it is hers to find.

choices.text: Show the first-year cost again, then explain how the provider bills for replication by the hour
choices.why: That answers a different question at length, and a long answer to a short question reads as nervousness.

choices.text: Say she does not know, write the question down where he sees it, and promise the figure by Thursday
choices.why: "I don't know; I will find out by Thursday" beats a guess, and a promise kept adds to the credibility of the whole proposal.

prompt: The labels most status page services use for an incident's public updates run: investigating, identified, ___, resolved.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 14.

prompt: The operations director asked Lívia for "a text message to every customer whose order is late", and they talked it through. Lívia writes back the same day. Which belong in her note? Choose all that apply.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 6.

choices.text: The need as Lívia understood it, set apart from the text message that had been asked for
choices.why: The request was a solution; the note names the need separately, so the message stays one option among several.

choices.text: What they agreed, with who will do what, and by which date
choices.why: A version both sides agreed to, written the same day, is the one both will point at when the work is delivered.

choices.text: A design of the messaging service, so that the director can approve it in her reply
choices.why: The note fixes what was heard and agreed; designing the requested solution before the need is confirmed skips the point of listening.

choices.text: A last line asking her to correct anything wrong by a named day
choices.why: The ask is what turns a summary into a check: memory of a conversation drifts, and differently for each person.

prompt: After a failed release, a company convenes a review that establishes which written procedure was broken, enters a formal correction against the team that broke it and files the report with the change board. Nobody is fired, and nobody outside the board reads the report. In Westrum's terms, which culture is that?
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 15.

choices.text: Bureaucratic: failure leads to justice, and the information goes through channels
choices.why: A rule found broken and a correction recorded is justice; a report filed with one board is information handled through channels.

choices.text: Generative: nobody was punished for it, so the failure was treated as an inquiry
choices.why: Generative failure leads to inquiry into how the system let it happen, and its reports are sought out by everybody, not filed.

choices.text: Pathological: a formal correction is scapegoating, whatever the tone of the meeting
choices.why: Pathological cultures shoot the messenger and hoard information; a procedure-based correction is the bureaucratic shape.

choices.text: Generative, provided the procedure is changed as well as the team corrected
choices.why: Changing the procedure would help, but a review that looks for the broken rule and the team that broke it is still seeking justice.

prompt: Each sentence below comes from a status note and carries a kind of word that does no work. Match each sentence to its kind.
hint: Communication, Consulting and Technical Leadership, lesson 1.

pairs.left: I just wanted to reach out with a quick update on the release.
It appears that it may possibly be the case that the cache is the cause.
We will carry out a review of the retry settings.
pairs.right: a verb hidden inside a noun

pairs.left: The rollback was decided last night.
pairs.right: a passive that hides who acted

right_distractors: repeating what the reader has just read

prompt: The library moves its availability read model to a projector that takes `CopyLent` events off a queue, with the `traceparent` riding in each message. On a busy morning the trace store lists lending traces as twenty-odd seconds long, and a manager concludes that lending has become slow. What do those traces actually say?
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 8; Observability and Operations, lesson 11.

choices.text: The desk's answer came when the root span ended; the rest is events waiting in the queue before the projector.
choices.why: Right: a trace is measured to its last span, and the wait in the queue has no span of its own. The customer's wait is the root span's duration.

choices.text: The command now waits for the projector before it returns, so every loan costs the desk those twenty seconds.
choices.why: Projected asynchronously, the command returns before any projector runs; freeing the write is the reason to project later.

choices.text: The seconds between the two services are clock skew, the noise to ignore in any trace that crosses two machines' clocks.
choices.why: Skew is a few milliseconds and can make a short wait look negative; a wait of seconds is a finding.

choices.text: The write model is twenty seconds behind, so `LendCopy` can lend a copy that is out until the projector catches up.
choices.why: The write model is never stale and refuses at once; only a screen read from the projection lags, provided no rule reads it.

prompt: An event-sourced library stores `MemberJoined` with the member's name and CPF, the way lesson 9's first event carries a name. A member asks to be erased under the LGPD, and the store's trigger refuses every `UPDATE`. Which design would have made her request answerable?
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 9; Observability and Operations, lesson 10.

choices.text: An upcaster that blanks the CPF whenever `MemberJoined` is read, so that the projections stop seeing it.
choices.why: An upcaster adapts the shape on the way out; the stored row still holds the CPF, in the store and in every backup of it.

choices.text: Events that name her by an internal id meaning nothing outside, with her name and CPF in a table that loses one row on demand.
choices.why: Right: the stream never held the person, so nothing append-only has to change. Deleting the row leaves the history joined to nobody.

choices.text: A migration that rewrites old `MemberJoined` events without the CPF, the way a table gains or loses a column.
choices.why: That is the fix lesson 9 rejects: the trigger refuses it, and a history that has been edited can no longer be trusted.

choices.text: Deleting every snapshot of her stream, so that the next rebuild folds a stream without her details.
choices.why: A snapshot is a cache of the fold; the events it came from still carry the CPF.

prompt: A stock service runs its shelves as actors under a supervisor tree, and its HTTP thread answers Kubernetes' liveness probe at `/health` with `{"status": "ok"}`. A malformed message keeps crashing one shelf until the root supervisor reaches its restart limit and gives up, and `/health` still answers `ok`. What should giving up at the root do?
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 17; Observability and Operations, lesson 14.

choices.text: Make the readiness probe fail, so traffic leaves the pod until a person restarts it by hand.
choices.why: Readiness moves traffic and restarts nothing; a pod whose actors are gone would sit out of rotation, alive and useless.

choices.text: Make liveness check the database as well, since the state that has to survive a crash lives there and a lost link is the likely cause.
choices.why: That is the probe that kills: a dependency in liveness restarts every copy when the database fails, and no restart helps.

choices.text: Fail the probe that decides on restarts, or end the process, so the platform starts a fresh container that clears the fault.
choices.why: Right: past its limit a supervisor escalates, and at the root the next level up is the container platform. What must survive lives outside the actors.

choices.text: Restart the shelf with no limit at all, because a fresh instance starts from a known good state each time.
choices.why: The same message crashes every fresh shelf, so a supervisor with no limit spins on it for ever.

prompt: The website's page views reach the weekly report through a bounded buffer that drops new values when it is full. Lesson 16 says that whatever the strategy, you count what it loses. Which instruments fit that advice? Choose all that apply.
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 16; Observability and Operations, lesson 6.

choices.text: A counter of drops labelled by `user_id`, so the report can say whose views went missing.
choices.why: One series per user is the cardinality lesson 6 measured; who was affected belongs in a log line or a trace.

choices.text: A counter, `pageviews_dropped_total`, incremented on every drop and read with `rate()`.
choices.why: Right: how many were lost is a question of how many happened, which is a counter's question.

choices.text: A gauge set to the number of drops since start-up, so that `rate()` gives drops per second.
choices.why: `rate()` of a gauge reads every fall as a restart, and a running total kept in a gauge is lost at every restart.

choices.text: A gauge of how many page views wait in the buffer right now, the number that reaches its limit first.
choices.why: Right: how many are there now is a gauge, and a buffer sitting at its limit is what comes before the drops.

prompt: A batch job looks up six ISBNs inside one trace, through the national catalogue wrapped twice: `CachingCatalogue(TracedCatalogue(national))`, where `TracedCatalogue` opens a span around each lookup. As in lesson 6's run, the national service is needed for three of the six. Jaeger shows three catalogue spans. Why three?
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 6; Observability and Operations, lesson 12.

choices.text: Head sampling dropped half of them, since `parentbased_traceidratio` keeps only a fraction of every trace.
choices.why: Sampling decides per trace and the flag travels with it, so the six lookups' spans are kept or dropped together.

choices.text: The proxy answers a repeat with the first lookup's span, and Jaeger merges the duplicates into one.
choices.why: No backend merges spans; a span exists only where some code opened one.

choices.text: Decorators commute, so the count follows the cache's size and not the order the two wrappers are in.
choices.why: Order is part of the rule: the inner wrapper only sees what the outer one lets through.

choices.text: The tracer sits inside the cache and only sees misses; wrap it outside to time every lookup.
choices.why: Right: the caching proxy answers repeats itself, so they never reach the wrapper it holds.

prompt: An internal `catalogue-client` package, imported by four services, should produce spans. Its author builds a `TracerProvider` with an OTLP exporter in the package's `__init__.py`, so that tracing works wherever the package is imported. What do the two courses say about that?
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 5; Observability and Operations, lesson 2.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong: without an SDK the API raises on the first span, so a library has to bring its own provider.
choices.why: Without an SDK the API hands back spans that record nothing and raise nothing, which is what lets a library ship instrumented.

choices.text: The library calls only the API; which provider and SDK will run is chosen once, in each service's composition root.
choices.why: Right: where spans go is configuration made once at start-up, and the library stays the same in every service.

choices.text: It should take a `Tracer` in every constructor, since `trace.get_tracer` is a service locator and those are always wrong.
choices.why: Lesson 5 tolerates a locator for cross-cutting services, as with `logging.getLogger`; the tracing API's global is that case.

choices.text: It is fine if the provider is built only when `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` is set, so a service opts out by leaving it unset.
choices.why: The choice still lives in a library, out of sight of each service's start-up, where it belongs and can be changed.

prompt: In lesson 9's event store, two clerks serving the same member make the second append fail with `ConcurrencyError`. To find which streams collide most, a developer adds `appends_conflicted_total{stream="member-bia"}`, one label value per member, in a library of twenty thousand members. What does the reviewer say?
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 9; Observability and Operations, lesson 6.

choices.text: That label makes one series per person; count by the command instead, and record the stream on the span that failed.
choices.why: Right: a label should take a small, known set of values, and what identifies one member belongs on a span or in a log line.

choices.text: Nothing: a counter just grows, and cardinality is a cost of gauges, which keep a last value per series.
choices.why: Every distinct label value is its own series whatever the type; lesson 6's twenty thousand series came from a counter.

choices.text: Nothing: a stream is the boundary of one decision, so it is the natural label for anything measured about it.
choices.why: That is a reason for how the store is designed, and it says nothing about what a series costs Prometheus.

choices.text: Drop the metric and log at `ERROR` instead, since a conflict means two clerks broke a rule and somebody has to act on it now.
choices.why: A conflict is the check working: the loser re-reads the stream and runs the rules again, an ordinary outcome.

prompt: Renewals are answered by the primary, which replicates to another region. Their latency SLI is the share answered within 100 ms, read from a bucket at `le="0.1"`. To stop the replica serving a stale due date, the team makes every commit wait for the replica. With lesson 10's figures, what happens to that SLI on a day when nothing fails?
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 10; Observability and Operations, lesson 15.

choices.text: Nothing: waiting for a replica costs time just while the network is partitioned, which is CAP's case.
choices.why: That is PACELC's else: with every link healthy, waiting for the replica cost 113 ms on every write.

choices.text: Nothing the SLI can see, because the histogram interpolates 113 ms into the bucket below the boundary.
choices.why: A share below a bucket boundary involves no interpolation; a 113 ms renewal lands above 0.1 and counts as bad.

choices.text: It rises, since a renewal can no longer be read stale from the replica, and stale reads counted as bad.
choices.why: A latency SLI counts durations against a threshold; staleness is not one of the events it measures.

choices.text: It falls to about zero: each renewal takes about 113 ms instead of 3, past the 100 ms boundary, with nothing broken.
choices.why: Right: consistency on a healthy day is paid in latency, and this objective says the team cannot afford it as written.

prompt: The shelf actor moves to another process, and only pickled values reach its mailbox, so the desk's current span cannot follow on its own. Before each `tell`, the desk calls `propagate.___(headers)` and puts the dictionary inside what it sends; the shelf calls `propagate.extract` on it before starting its span.
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 17; Observability and Operations, lesson 4.

prompt: The shelf actor moves to another machine, and the desk's messages now reach it through Envoy, which retries a 5xx from the shelf up to twice. What must the design now allow for? Choose all that apply.
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 17; Observability and Operations, lesson 19.

choices.text: A lend that arrives twice, since a retried message is a duplicate the shelf's handler has to recognise.
choices.why: Right: across a network a retried message arrives twice, and a retry is only safe if the request is.

choices.text: Exactly-once delivery, which the retries now give: a remote tell that failed is sent again by Envoy.
choices.why: Retries add duplicates and do not remove loss; remote actor systems promise at most once by default, Akka included.

choices.text: A page on the shelf's own error ratio, since Envoy's retries hide every failure from the desk's numbers.
choices.why: With the failure invisible to users, that page wakes somebody for nothing; page on the symptom at the edge, keep causes as tickets.

choices.text: A shelf that has gone silent, which from the desk looks the same as a slow one and is found by a timeout.
choices.why: Right: at a distance, failure is detected by timeout, because silence and slowness look alike.

prompt: The rules in `notices.py` call a vendor's APM library directly to record each overdue notice, and the company is weighing a move to another vendor. Following both courses, where should the vendor's code live?
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 4; Observability and Operations, lesson 13.

choices.text: In the rules, behind `if VENDOR == ...` branches, so that switching vendor becomes a one-line change of a setting.
choices.why: The middle then imports every edge it might ever use, which is the one import ports and adapters forbids.

choices.text: In each service's own agent, since every product accepts OTLP now and a tool can strip an agent's calls later.
choices.why: Accepting OTLP removes no vendor call from the code; that lock-in comes out line by line.

choices.text: At the edge: the rules call OpenTelemetry's API, and the vendor is an exporter in the Collector.
choices.why: Right: nothing in the middle imports the edge, and a change of vendor becomes a change of configuration.

choices.text: In the rules, which should import the SDK and the exporter themselves, so the wiring sits visibly beside the logic.
choices.why: Lesson 4's rule about imports is that nothing in the middle imports anything at the edge; wiring belongs at the root.

prompt: A team of four runs five Python services and proposes Istio, saying it is what serious platforms run. No regulator asks for encryption between services, and nobody needs canaries by percentage. Which argument do both courses support?
hint: Design Patterns and Principles, lesson 19; Observability and Operations, lesson 19.

choices.text: Name the force first: a mesh pays for many teams and languages, required mTLS or traffic control, and none is here.
choices.why: Right: a pattern earns its indirection when it absorbs a change that costs more than the hops, and this one absorbs none yet.

choices.text: Adopt it now, since a proxy costs 17 MB and under half a per cent of a CPU, negligible at any scale.
choices.why: The overhead grows with the number of pods, and the control plane is a critical system somebody has to run.

prompt: The library adds `Periodical(Item)`, whose `lend` raises `ValueError` for an issue less than a month old, while `Item.lend` lends any item. Which shape of substitution failure is this, and where does the repair go?

choices.text: A weakened postcondition, like `Laptop`; relax the parent's promise about due dates for every caller.
choices.why: A weakened postcondition returns something the parent ruled out; this child refuses something the parent accepted.

choices.text: A broken invariant, like `Square`; the repair is to give `Item` no setters, so nothing changes a periodical.
choices.why: No state ends up where the parent forbade it; the call is refused before anything changes.

choices.text: No failure: raising is louder than a wrong answer, so callers catching `ValueError` suffice.
choices.why: A refusal is the first shape, `ReferenceBook`'s, and a catch in every caller is the repair the lesson rules out.

choices.text: A strengthened precondition, as with `ReferenceBook`; repair what the hierarchy claims, not the callers.
choices.why: Right: a new issue is not lendable, so `Periodical` should not claim to be an item that lends it.

choices.text: The counter is shared by every instance, so the report read the count of a different shelf object.

choices.text: The child relied on the parent's self-call to `add`, which a correct change removed.

choices.text: The change broke the parent's own tests, which nobody ran before the report.
choices.why: Every test of `Shelf` still passes; the shelf holds four titles, and the parent did nothing wrong by its own rules.

prompt: When a book comes back, `publish` walks a plain list of three listeners: fines, e-mail and statistics. While the e-mail listener talks to the mail server, another thread unsubscribes fines. The statistics never hear of the return, and nothing is raised. What fix does lesson 18 give?

choices.text: Hold the lock for the whole of `publish`, so nobody can unsubscribe while listeners run.

choices.text: Start a thread per listener in `publish`, so a slow e-mail no longer holds the walk open.
choices.why: The walk is still over a list another thread can change; more threads give the race more chances.
