choices.why: An image fixes its bytes when it is built; every photo uploaded after the build would still live on one machine.

choices.text: Set `ignore_changes = [ami]`, so that Terraform stops replacing the group's machines
choices.why: The group, not Terraform, ended those instances when it scaled in; a lifecycle setting does not stop a scale-in.

choices.text: Only the image survives: uploads belong in object storage, fixes in the template
choices.why: Nothing written on a machine outlives it, so the data leaves the machine and a fix ships as a new image version.

prompt: A company that runs on AWS buys one that runs on Google Cloud, and both estates stay where they are. The architect wants one infrastructure-as-code tool for the two clouds, the DNS provider and the GitHub organisation. Which choice, with which expectation, fits the two lessons?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 17; Cloud and Serverless, lesson 2.

choices.text: Terraform or OpenTofu; each cloud keeps its own identity system and its bill
choices.why: They reach anything with a provider, and the tool does not merge the clouds: two identity systems and two bills remain.

choices.text: CloudFormation, which keeps the state inside the provider and leaves none to lose
choices.why: CloudFormation reaches AWS only; it cannot hold the Google Cloud estate, the DNS or GitHub.

choices.text: The AWS CDK in TypeScript, as a general-purpose language can describe either cloud
choices.why: The CDK writes CloudFormation templates, so it reaches AWS and nothing else.

choices.text: Terraform, so that one configuration lets the application fail over between clouds
choices.why: Failing over between providers needs the application running on both and its data copied between them; the cloud lesson calls it the most expensive reason.

prompt: A virtual machine carries a role that may write backups to one bucket. Match each set-up on the machine to whom the AWS CLI there ends up calling as.
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 7.

pairs.left: Nothing else is configured on the machine
pairs.right: the role, through the instance metadata service

pairs.left: `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and its secret are exported in the shell
`~/.aws/credentials` holds a key, and the shell exports none
pairs.right: the owner of the key in that file

pairs.left: The role is taken off, and nothing else is configured
pairs.right: nobody: `NoCredentials`, and no request is sent

right_distractors: the role, since the machine's own source is read first

prompt: Two pipeline jobs run against the shop's S3 backend a minute apart. The second fails at once with `Error acquiring the state lock`, and `Who` names the first job's runner, which is healthy and still applying. What does lesson 7 give the pipeline for this?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 7.

choices.text: `terraform force-unlock` with the printed `ID`, run by the second job before it plans
choices.why: The holder is alive; forcing the lock lets a second writer in beside it, the lost update the lock exists to stop.

choices.text: `-lock=false` on plans, because a plan writes nothing to AWS and needs no lock
choices.why: Plans lock too: reading a state while another run writes it gives a plan of a world that never existed.

choices.text: `-lock-timeout`, so the later job waits its turn and plans on top of the earlier one's work
choices.why: With a timeout of a few minutes, two jobs that collided become two jobs that ran in turn.

choices.text: A `dynamodb_table` in the backend, so that each of the jobs can hold a lock of its own
choices.why: The table is the older home of the same single lock, deprecated in favour of `use_lockfile`; it never gave two writers a lock each.

prompt: In the lesson's GitHub workflow, a job can ask GitHub for the token that `configure-aws-credentials` exchanges for a role's credentials only when its `permissions` include `id-token: ___`.
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 15.

prompt: After the shop is split into a network state and an app state, four needs come up. Match each one to the tool lesson 8 gives it.
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 8.

pairs.left: The app's security group needs the VPC id, and the app may read the network's state
The app needs two network values, and may not download the network's state
pairs.right: an SSM parameter the network writes for others to read

pairs.left: The data team takes over a bucket that the app's state manages
pairs.right: a `removed` block in the app, then an `import` block in theirs

pairs.left: A security group made by hand, with rules nobody wrote down, must join the app's state
pairs.right: an `import` block, and a plan that drafts the block for you

right_distractors: a `moved` block that names the data team's state
`terraform state rm` in the app, and nothing more

prompt: Applying Ana's saved `tfplan` stopped halfway: the batch security group was created, and the API refused the subnet's range. She corrects the range in `main.tf` and runs `terraform apply tfplan` again. What happens?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 9.

choices.text: It applies the corrected range, since `apply` reads the `main.tf` beside the plan file
choices.why: A saved plan carries the configuration it was computed from, and this one is refused before anything is read.

choices.text: It deletes the security group first, so the plan can start again from nothing
choices.why: An apply is not a transaction: what succeeded stays in AWS and in the state, and nothing is rolled back.

choices.text: It creates the security group again, and then the subnet and the instance
choices.why: The state already records the group, and the file is refused before any of this.

choices.text: It refuses the file as stale; a new plan proposes only the subnet and the instance
choices.why: The failed apply wrote the state, so the saved plan is spent; a fresh plan finds the two things still missing.

prompt: After a provider's version constraint is raised in `versions.tf`, the lock file keeps pinning the old version, and plans stop, until somebody runs `terraform init -___`, whose diff of `.terraform.lock.hcl` then belongs in the review.
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 9.

prompt: Ana's root calls the network module as `module "shop"`, from `./modules/network`, and her state holds `module.shop.aws_vpc.this` and its subnets. Which of these edits leave every address in the state as it is? Choose all that apply.
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 10.

choices.text: Renaming the call to `module "network"`, keeping the same source and arguments
choices.why: The call's label is the first part of every address, so each one changes and the plan destroys and creates.

choices.text: Pointing `source` at the same files under a Git tag, then running `terraform init`
choices.why: Where a module's files come from is not part of the address; the lesson's plan said `No changes`.

choices.text: Renaming `aws_subnet.this` to `aws_subnet.private` inside the module, without `moved`
choices.why: The resource's name is part of the address; without a `moved` block the subnets are destroyed and created.

choices.text: Moving the `module` block out of `main.tf` into a new `network.tf` beside it
choices.why: Terraform reads every `.tf` file in the directory as one configuration; which file holds a block is for the reader.

prompt: The network module's author renames `aws_subnet.this` to `aws_subnet.private` without making any caller rebuild a subnet. Put the steps in order, from the author's branch to a caller's clean plan.
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 10.
items: On a branch, rename the resource and its reference in `outputs.tf`
Add `moved.tf`, from `aws_subnet.this` to `aws_subnet.private`
Merge the branch into `main` and tag the merge `v1.1.0`
Push `main` and the tag to the module's repository
In the caller, move both `?ref=` to `v1.1.0` and run `terraform init`
Read the plan: only `has moved to` lines, nothing added or destroyed
trap: Tagging `v1.1.0` before `moved.tf` is on the branch is the slip: a published tag is never moved, so callers who take it plan three subnets destroyed and three created, and the fix needs yet another version.

prompt: A pull request changes both web servers in `web.tf` from `t3.medium` to `t3.micro`, and keeps their 20 GB `gp3` root disks. What `change per month, USD` does lesson 16's `price.py` print for its plan?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 16.

prompt: An Auto Scaling group carries `ignore_changes = [desired_capacity]`, because an autoscaler moves that number all day and the file holds only the starting value. At noon, with the autoscaler well above that value, a merged change forces the group to be replaced. What capacity does the new group start with?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 6.

choices.text: The autoscaler's noon value, which Terraform kept in the state and carries over
choices.why: Terraform reads the ignored value into the state, but a new resource is created from the file.

choices.text: The file's starting value, as ignored arguments come from it on creation
choices.why: `ignore_changes` applies only after creation; a replacement is a creation, and the file decides.

choices.text: None yet: Terraform refuses to replace a resource that has an ignored argument
choices.why: Ignoring an argument stops a comparison; it does not stop a replacement forced by another argument.

choices.text: The old group's capacity, which `create_before_destroy` copies to the new one
choices.why: Lifecycle settings change the order of the two steps; they copy no values between objects.

prompt: To save snapshot storage, the image pipeline deregisters the previous `shop-web` AMI on the day a new version ships. Then `1.1.0` turns out to be faulty, and Ana runs lesson 20's rollback. What happens?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 20.

choices.text: `git revert` restores `1.0.1`, the lookup by name finds no image, and the plan fails
choices.why: The rollback works only because the old AMI still exists, which is why a pipeline keeps the last few versions.

choices.text: Terraform starts the new instance from a copy of the old image kept in its state
choices.why: The state records an AMI's id, not the image; with the image gone there is nothing to start.

choices.text: The plan updates the running instance in place, back to the older image's files
choices.why: A different `ami` forces a replacement, and there is no older image to replace it with.

choices.text: Nothing breaks: the old instance waits as a deposed object, ready to come back
choices.why: The deposed object was destroyed in the same apply that created its replacement.

prompt: Ana's play gains a second template task, which writes a TLS snippet into nginx's configuration and also notifies `Reload nginx`. On the next run both files change on `web1`. When is nginx reloaded there, and how often?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 18.

choices.text: Twice, each one right after the task that notified the handler
choices.why: A notified handler does not run where it was notified; it waits for the end of the play.

choices.text: Once, right after the first task that reported a change
choices.why: A notified handler does not run where it was notified; it waits for the end of the play.

choices.text: Once, at the end of the play, after every one of its tasks has run
choices.why: A handler runs only when notified and only once, at the end of the play, however many tasks notified it.

choices.text: Twice, at the end of the play, one for each notifying task
choices.why: Two notifications of one handler still give one run.

prompt: Security forbids any connection into the shop's servers, SSH from a control machine included. The team still wants a configuration change to reach every server at once, not on the next half-hourly run. Which arrangement from lesson 19 fits?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 19.

choices.text: Ansible run from a control machine, which installs nothing at all on the servers
choices.why: Push needs the control machine to reach every target over SSH, which is the connection security forbids.

choices.text: `salt-ssh`, which reaches every server without a minion installed on it
choices.why: It works over SSH as well, an inbound connection to each server.

choices.text: Puppet agents on their defaults, which open the connection from the inside
choices.why: They do connect outwards, but every 1800 seconds: a change waits for the next run.

choices.text: Salt minions, which open the connection themselves and run what is published
choices.why: The minion keeps its own connection to the master open, and what the master publishes runs at once.

prompt: The shop's subnets use `for_each` over a map keyed `web`, `app` and `db`. A tidy-up renames the key `db` to `data` and keeps the same range. What does the plan propose, and what keeps the subnet as it is?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 4.

choices.text: It destroys `app["db"]` and creates `app["data"]`; a `moved` block pairing them keeps it
choices.why: An address is the only thing Terraform matches on, and `moved` tells it that `aws_subnet.app["db"]` is now `aws_subnet.app["data"]`.

choices.text: Nothing: the range is unchanged, so Terraform finds the same subnet under the new key
choices.why: Terraform does not look at ranges to pair objects; it matches addresses.

choices.text: An update in place of the subnet's key, because a key is only a name
choices.why: The key is part of the address in the state, not an argument AWS can update.

choices.text: It replaces all three subnets, because changing one key shifts the others
choices.why: That is `count`'s index problem; the other keys of a map stay where they are.

prompt: A unit test runs under `mock_provider "aws" {}` and asserts that `aws_vpc.this.arn` contains `sa-east-1`. No override sets the ARN. What happens, and why?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 13.

choices.text: It passes: the mock keeps the provider's schema, so the ARN looks like AWS's
choices.why: The schema says which attributes exist; the values of the computed ones are invented.

choices.text: It is skipped, because a mock cannot give a value to a computed attribute
choices.why: A run is skipped when its provider cannot be configured or a run before it failed; a mock gives every computed attribute a value.

choices.text: It fails: a mock fills each computed attribute with eight random characters
choices.why: Under a mock only what the module sets and what an override supplies means anything; the ARN in the lesson's run was `jhm1adza`.

choices.text: It passes only when the AWS endpoint answers, as the mock asks it for the ARN
choices.why: A mock never calls the provider's API; the lesson ran it with the endpoint pointing at nothing.

prompt: To try a change in dev, a colleague stands in `~/shop-infra/live`, the folder that holds both `dev` and `prod`, runs `terragrunt run --all apply`, and answers `y` to the one question. What does Terragrunt do?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 11.

choices.text: It applies dev's units only, because dev is where the change was made
choices.why: `run --all` takes every unit below the current directory, whatever changed.

choices.text: It applies every unit below `live`, prod's too, with `-auto-approve`
choices.why: That one question is the only confirmation the whole queue gets: the classic mistake the lesson's table gives Terragrunt.

choices.text: It asks again before each unit's apply, as a plain `terraform apply` would
choices.why: Under `run --all`, Terragrunt adds `-auto-approve` to every command unless told `--no-auto-approve`.

choices.text: It refuses: units run only from their own folder, never from `root.hcl`'s
choices.why: `run --all` is meant to run from a folder above the units; the lesson ran it from `live/dev`.

prompt: A reporting service calls a partner's API and, every few days, starts logging `Too many open files` until somebody restarts it. `ls -l /proc/PID/fd | wc -l` sits close to the unit's `LimitNOFILE=`, and `ss -tn` on the host lists thousands of connections to the partner in `CLOSE-WAIT`. The team proposes raising the limit. What do the two courses say?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6; Networks and Protocols, lesson 3.

choices.text: The partner closed them and the program never closed its side: a leak that a higher limit only postpones.
choices.why: Every connection is a descriptor, and `CLOSE-WAIT` that piles up is a program that forgets to close what the other side already closed.

choices.text: `CLOSE-WAIT` is what every busy client shows for sixty seconds after each call it makes, so a higher limit is the right fix.
choices.why: That is `TIME-WAIT`, on the side that closed first; `CLOSE-WAIT` means the other side closed and this program has not.

choices.text: The partner's firewall drops the closing packets, so each connection waits out a timeout that a higher limit can ride through.
choices.why: A drop shows as waiting in `SYN-SENT` or a timeout; here the partner's close arrived, which is exactly what `CLOSE-WAIT` records.

choices.text: Sockets are not files, so the descriptors are something else and the connections are another matter.
choices.why: A TCP connection is not in the filesystem, but it is still an entry in the same descriptor table that `LimitNOFILE=` caps.

prompt: The checkout API is slow. On its host, `vmstat 1 5` shows nothing in `r` or `b` and `id` near 100, `free -m` has plenty `available`, and `iostat -xz` is quiet. From that host, `curl -w` with lesson 5's five timers against the pricing service it calls shows `dns`, `tcp` and `tls` done within a few milliseconds, and `first byte` arriving seconds later. Where is the fix?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11; Networks and Protocols, lesson 5.

choices.text: On the checkout host: idle processors with a slow API mean the scheduler is starving it, and more cores will cure that.
choices.why: An idle machine that is still slow is not this machine; adding cores to it changes nothing the timers measured.

choices.text: In the network between the two: seconds before the first byte are distance or loss on the path.
choices.why: Distance and loss show in `tcp` and `tls`, which needs round trips; both were quick here.

choices.text: In the code of the service being called: the network answered at once, and the wait begins once the request lands.
choices.why: A slow first byte after everything else was quick is the application thinking, and the idle host had already said it was not this machine.

choices.text: In the TLS setup: a new handshake on every call is the cost, and reusing connections removes it.
choices.why: The handshake finished within milliseconds of `tcp`; the seconds come after it, while the server works on the answer.

prompt: A nightly copy between two servers in the same rack now takes many times longer than it used to, and nothing reports a failure. `ss -ti` on the copy's connection shows `retrans` climbing, and `ip -s link show eth0` on the receiver shows its `errors` counter growing. The proposal on the table is larger machines with faster disks. What do the two courses point at?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11; Networks and Protocols, lesson 3.

choices.text: Retransmissions happen on every network, so those counters are noise and the disks are the real bottleneck.
choices.why: On the internet they are ordinary; between two machines in one rack, retransmissions mean something on the link is broken.

choices.text: A cable or a card is damaging frames on that link, and TCP turns each loss into a wait, not an error.
choices.why: `errors` counts malformed frames, a cable or a card, and TCP resends what was lost, so the copy finishes late instead of failing.

choices.text: The receiving program reads too slowly, and the sender keeps repeating segments until the reader catches up.
choices.why: A slow reader leaves bytes waiting in `Recv-Q`; a retransmission is a segment that was never acknowledged, and `errors` is the card's count.

choices.text: The copy should move to UDP, which skips the acknowledgements and so never has anything to send twice.
choices.why: A copy needs every byte in order, which is TCP's job; UDP would lose the same frames and simply not notice.

prompt: On `ops1`, `ss -tulpn` lists the internal admin page on `127.0.0.1:8080`. A colleague wants it moved to `0.0.0.0:8080` so the team can open it from their laptops. Which way gives the team the page and leaves the listener where it is?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11; Networks and Protocols, lesson 7.

choices.text: `ssh -f -N -R 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 ops1`, so that the server's port leads to the page
choices.why: `-R` is the mirror image: a port on the server leads back to the client, which is the wrong direction here.

choices.text: `ssh -f -N -L 8080:ops1:8080 ops1`, since `127.0.0.1` inside the tunnel would mean the laptop
choices.why: The destination is read on the server, where `127.0.0.1` is the server itself; the page listens on no other address.
sshd makes the last connection on `ops1`, so `127.0.0.1` there is the server itself, and the page never listens on the network.

choices.text: Moving it is fine, because `0.0.0.0` accepts connections from the machine's own programs alone
choices.why: It is the other way round: `0.0.0.0` is every address the machine has, which is what makes a service exposed.

prompt: On a build server every developer logs into, the deploy job wrote the shop's TLS private key under the shell's default umask, `0022`. For months it has sat as `-rw-r--r--` in a `drwxr-xr-x` directory. What do the two courses have you do now?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4; Networks and Protocols, lesson 6.

choices.text: `chmod 600` on the key is enough, because the mode is checked again on every read from now on.
choices.why: It stops the next read, not the ones already made, and a key anybody could read for months has to be treated as leaked.

choices.text: Set `umask 077` on the server; it tightens the files that already exist as well as the new ones.
choices.why: A umask applies when a file is created and never again; the key keeps its `644`.

choices.text: Nothing urgent: the server hands the key to every visitor in the handshake, so reading it gives nobody anything new.
choices.why: The certificate is what every visitor gets; the key never leaves the server, and whoever holds it can be the server.

choices.text: Treat it as leaked: a new key and a new certificate, with the next key born `600` under `umask 077`.
choices.why: A leaked key means somebody else can be this server, and the only fix is a new key and certificate; `077` makes the file private from its first moment.

prompt: The edge proxies are switched off at night to save money, and their certificates are renewed by a crontab line at `03:00`. The CA/Browser Forum has voted to bring the longest certificate down to 47 days by 2029. What should the renewal run from?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 13; Networks and Protocols, lesson 6.

choices.text: The same crontab line: a 47-day certificate is due once every 47 days, and cron will hit one of them.
choices.why: Cron loses every run the machine was off for, and a renewal is meant to happen well before the end, not on the last day.

choices.text: A systemd timer with `Persistent=true`, so a run missed while the machine was off happens at boot.
choices.why: Missed runs are lost to cron and caught by `Persistent=true`; renewing automatically, a month ahead, is what makes short certificates bearable.

choices.text: A monthly reminder to renew by hand, which is shorter than the certificate's life.
choices.why: A certificate renewed by hand is the one that expires on a Sunday, and shorter lives make that more likely, not less.

choices.text: The crontab line with `RandomizedDelaySec=30m` added, so that the run lands after the machine is back.
choices.why: That is a timer setting cron cannot express, and a random delay spreads a fleet out rather than waiting for a machine to boot.

prompt: On a new build server inside the company network, `apt update` prints `403  Forbidden [IP: 185.125.189.187 443]` for two PPAs, then says each repository `is no longer signed`. A teammate wants to re-import the PPAs' signing keys. What do the two courses say?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 7; Networks and Protocols, lesson 5.

choices.text: The company's proxy answered and refused; a key fault would read `NO_PUBKEY`, so ask the proxy's owners.
choices.why: A `403` is a finished conversation in which the server declined, and apt's message names the consequence, not the cause.

choices.text: The signing keys have expired, which is exactly what `no longer signed` names, so new keys will bring the PPAs back.
choices.why: `no longer signed` appears whenever the signed index is missing, whatever the reason; the `Failed to fetch` line above it says `403`.

choices.text: A firewall on the way drops the connections to port 443, and apt reports the timeout that follows as a `403`.
choices.why: A drop leaves the client waiting with no answer at all; a status code means something received the request and replied.

choices.text: The PPA names no longer resolve on this network, and `403` is the way apt words a lookup that found nothing.
choices.why: The line carries the address it reached, `185.125.189.187`; DNS had answered and the request had arrived.

prompt: A site built on a developer's Mac works there. On the Linux server the pages load without their styles, and the log shows `404` for `/css/Header.css`; the file in the repository is `header.css`. What is the cause?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 1.

choices.text: Linux decides a file's type by its extension, and `.css` was never registered on the server.
choices.why: The extension is part of the name and nothing else; there is no registry of types for it to be missing from.

choices.text: On Linux `Header.css` and `header.css` are two different names, and only one of them exists.
choices.why: The Mac treated the two spellings as one file; the Linux filesystem does not, so the capitalised one is missing.

choices.text: The file was saved with Windows line endings, and the server refuses to send a file that has them.
choices.why: Line endings change what is inside a file, not whether its name is found; this request found no file at all.

choices.text: A capital letter at the front marks a file as hidden on Linux, and the web server skips hidden files.
choices.why: What hides a name is a leading dot, and only `ls` honours it; a capital letter hides nothing.

prompt: A security scanner flags every server on an Ubuntu LTS release, because their `nginx 1.18` is older than the upstream version that fixed a published flaw. The team proposes building nginx from source to get a newer number. What does lesson 2 say to do first?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 2.

choices.text: Accept the scanner's word: a fixed release gets no fixes of any kind until its next version comes out.
choices.why: A fixed release still receives security fixes; it freezes features, not patches.

choices.text: Move the servers to a rolling distribution, which is the release model that gets security fixes.
choices.why: Rolling gets today's software and changes under you; fixed releases get security fixes too, and production rarely rolls.

choices.text: Ask the package manager whether the fix is in: a fixed release backports without moving the number.
choices.why: Backporting applies the fix to the old version, so a scanner that only compares numbers reports problems that are not there.

choices.text: Move to the newest interim release, which carries both the newest nginx and the longest support.
choices.why: An interim release is supported for nine months, the shortest of Ubuntu's windows.

prompt: A packaging step runs `ln -s /build/shop/releases/new /build/shop/current` and archives `/build/shop`. The servers unpack the archive into `/srv/shop`, and `current` there points at nothing. Which link would have survived the move?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 3.

choices.text: A hard link, `ln /build/shop/releases/new current`, since it keeps working when the path changes.
choices.why: `releases/new` is a directory, and a hard link to a directory is forbidden.

choices.text: The same link, copied with `cp -r` instead of archived, because `cp` follows links as it goes.
choices.why: `cp -r` copies the link itself unless told `-L`, and the copied link stores the same absolute path.

choices.text: The same link, followed by `readlink -f current` on each server to rewrite it for its new place.
choices.why: `readlink -f` only prints where a chain of links ends; it changes nothing, and here it would end nowhere.

choices.text: `ln -s releases/new current`, run inside `/build/shop`: a relative link resolves from its own directory.
choices.why: A symlink stores the path it was given; a relative one survives the whole tree moving, and the absolute one points at `/build`, which the servers lack.

prompt: To make nginx restart after a crash, a colleague copied the packaged unit to `/etc/systemd/system/nginx.service` and changed one line. Months later the package shipped a fix to its unit, and this server still runs without it. Why, and what should the change have been?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5.

choices.text: The copy in `/etc` replaces the packaged unit and stops getting its fixes; `systemctl edit nginx` writes a drop-in.
choices.why: A drop-in is merged on top of the package's unit, so the package keeps updating underneath it.

choices.text: `/usr/lib/systemd/system` takes priority, so the package's fix already won, and the server only needs `daemon-reload`.
choices.why: The list runs highest first, and `/etc/systemd/system` sits above the package's directory; that is why the copy wins.

choices.text: apt leaves the unit files of a running service untouched, and the fix will arrive with the machine's next reboot.
choices.why: The package did update its own file in `/usr/lib`; the copy in `/etc` shadows it whether the machine reboots or not.

choices.text: When it was copied the unit lost its `[Install]` section, so it became `static` and systemd stopped rereading it.
choices.why: `[Install]` is read only by `systemctl enable`; a copy keeps it, and being `static` has nothing to do with updates.

prompt: A long import was started over ssh with `./import.sh &`, and an hour in the laptop's Wi-Fi dropped. Put what happened to the import in order.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6.
items: The ssh connection drops, and the terminal goes with it
The kernel sends `SIGHUP` to the session leader, the shell
Bash, on its way out, sends `SIGHUP` to its jobs
The import takes the default action for `SIGHUP`, and dies
trap: Having the kernel signal the import directly skips the one step that is not the kernel's: bash passes the hangup on to its jobs, which is why `disown` saves a job and `nohup` makes it ignore the signal.

prompt: On lesson 8's `access.log`, 1200 requests long, an alert for client errors was built on `grep -c ' 4[0-9][0-9] '`, which prints `80`. `awk '$9 >= 400 && $9 < 500' logs/access.log | wc -l` prints `54`. Counted correctly, what percentage of the requests got a `4xx` status?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 8.

prompt: A cleanup script holds `p=/var/log/nginx/access.log.1`. Match each expansion to what it prints, by lesson 9.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 9.

prompt: A nightly PowerShell job picks the `.log` files out of a large folder on a file server across the network with `Get-ChildItem | Where-Object { $_.Name -like '*.log' }`, and it takes about a minute. Which change does lesson 10 recommend?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 10.

choices.text: `Where-Object { $_.Name -match '\.log$' }`, because a regular expression is cheaper to test than a glob.
choices.why: Either comparison runs on every object after it is built; the time goes into building objects that are then thrown away.

choices.text: `Where-Object { $_.Name -clike '*.log' }`, since a comparison that minds case has less work to do.
choices.why: `-clike` changes what matches, not how many objects are made first; the folder is still read in full.

choices.text: `Get-ChildItem -Filter '*.log'`, so that the provider does the filtering and fewer objects are built.
choices.why: Filtering as far left as the command allows lets the file server send only what matches.

choices.text: `Get-ChildItem | Sort-Object Name` first, so that `Where-Object` can stop after the last `.log` name.
choices.why: `Where-Object` tests every object it receives, sorted or not, and sorting adds a pass over all of them.

prompt: On a server, `/etc/hosts` needs one line changed. The way lesson 12 calls correct copies the file, runs your own editor as you on the copy, and then installs the result as root: `___ /etc/hosts`.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 12.

prompt: A team keeps all its scheduled jobs in crontabs. By lesson 13, which of these are reasons to make one job a systemd timer instead? Choose all that apply.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 13.

choices.text: The machine is an Alpine container with no systemd in it
choices.why: A machine without systemd is one of the cases where the lesson says to stay with cron.

choices.text: A slow run must not overlap the next one
choices.why: An active service is not started again, so a timer prevents the overlap that cron leaves to you.

choices.text: Somebody who is not the author will have to read the schedule
choices.why: For a reader who is not you, the lesson prefers cron: five fields beat forty settings.

choices.text: The machine is off some nights, and a missed run should still happen
choices.why: Cron loses a missed run; `Persistent=true` runs it at boot.

prompt: In lesson 2's ping from the laptop to `192.0.2.80`, the web server sent its echo reply with a TTL of 64, and the laptop received it with `ttl=61`. How many routers did the reply cross?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 2.

prompt: A batch client on Linux opens a new TCP connection for every call to one database address and port, and always closes first. Its kernel picks source ports from `32768   60999`, like lesson 2's laptop, and each closed connection keeps its port in `TIME-WAIT` for the 60 seconds lesson 3 gives Linux. Sustained, about how many new connections per second can it open before it runs out of source ports?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lessons 2 and 3.

prompt: Over one night, a health probe running `dig` logged four different `status` values. Match each to whose problem lesson 4 says it is.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 4.

pairs.left: `NXDOMAIN`
pairs.right: a typo, or a record nobody created

pairs.left: `NOERROR` with `ANSWER: 0`
pairs.right: usually nobody's: the name has no record of that type

pairs.left: `REFUSED`
`SERVFAIL`

right_distractors: the resolver's cache, which needs a flush

prompt: A resolver with an empty cache is asked for `www.example.com`. Put the steps of its walk in order, as lesson 4's `dig +trace` prints them.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 4.
items: It finds the servers that answer for `.`, the root
The root, which does not know the name, refers it to the servers for `.com`
The `.com` server refers it to `ns1.example.com`
`ns1.example.com` answers with the `A` record, `192.0.2.80`
The resolver answers its client and keeps the record until the TTL runs out
trap: Starting at `ns1.example.com`, or expecting the root to know the address: each server answers only for its own part of the name and hands the rest down, so the walk begins at the root and ends at the one server that holds the zone.

prompt: A design review asks what the internet provider can see when a customer fetches `https://www.example.com/prices.txt`. By what lesson 5 captured on the office router, which of these can it read? Choose all that apply.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 5.

choices.text: The path, `/prices.txt`, which travels in the request line
choices.why: Over HTTPS the request line is encrypted; not one of the 36 packets contained `GET` or `prices`.

choices.text: The answer's headers, as the `Location:` line was in the plain capture
choices.why: That capture was plain HTTP; over HTTPS the answer's headers are inside the encryption with the rest.

choices.text: The name `www.example.com`, sent in the Client hello
choices.why: The server needs the name before any key exists, so it travels in the clear.

choices.text: The server's address, `192.0.2.80`
choices.why: Addresses are on every packet, and HTTPS does not hide which site was visited.

prompt: After a release, `https://www.example.com/app/` answers `502`, and nginx's error log says `connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream`, naming `127.0.0.1:9000`. The on-call engineer is about to restart nginx. What does lesson 5 tell you?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 5.

choices.text: Restart it: a `502` is nginx failing, and the refused connection in the log is its own socket.
choices.why: nginx accepted the request and answered it; the refusal came from the address it was passing the request on to.

choices.text: The path between the visitor and nginx is losing packets, which is what a gateway error reports.
choices.why: The status itself proves DNS, TCP, TLS and the request all worked; loss would have slowed them, not produced a code.

choices.text: The upstream's certificate failed to verify, and nginx logs a failed check as a refused connection.
choices.why: `111: Connection refused` is the TCP answer of lesson 3: nothing listens on that port, and no certificate was ever reached.

choices.text: nginx is healthy; the application behind it on port 9000 is not running, and that is where to look.
choices.why: A `502` means the web server could not reach the application behind it, so restarting nginx changes nothing.

prompt: A colleague sends the office CA's certificate, and its SHA-256 fingerprint matches the one read out over the phone. On Ubuntu it is copied into `/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/`, and then `sudo ___` adds it to the bundle that `curl` reads.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 6.

prompt: A security review of a cloud image finds `PasswordAuthentication no` appended to the end of `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`. `sshd -t` raises nothing and the service was reloaded, yet the server still accepts passwords. What does lesson 7 check, and what will it most likely show?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 7.

choices.text: `sshd -T`, the settings in force: a file in `sshd_config.d`, read first, says `yes`, and the first value wins.
choices.why: Ubuntu reads `sshd_config.d/*.conf` before the rest of the main file, so a `no` appended at the end changes nothing.

choices.text: `sshd -t -f` again, since a reload rereads only the files that were checked before it.
choices.why: `-t` only checks syntax; it says nothing about which value of a setting the server ends up using.

choices.text: The client's `~/.ssh/config`, which can force password logins even after the server has turned them off.
choices.why: The server decides which methods it accepts; with passwords off it answers `Permission denied (publickey)` to any client.

choices.text: `journalctl -u ssh`, where the reload will have logged that the appended line was ignored.
choices.why: Nothing is logged as ignored: the file is valid, and the earlier value simply took precedence.

prompt: In a design review, a developer who took the SQL course's lesson 2 to heart points at `dim_book`: the department's name is written on 1,185 rows, and it depends on the book only by way of the category, which is a transitive dependency. He wants a `dim_department` table. What answers him?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 2; Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 6.

choices.text: His premise fails: the department is computed from the whole key, `book_key`, so the dependency is not transitive.
choices.why: It is computed by way of the category, which is exactly the chain 3NF forbids. The star breaks the rule on purpose.

choices.text: 3NF's anomalies need many writers; `dim_book` has one, the load, which copies each name from one source.
choices.why: Right. The load rewrites all 1,185 rows from the source's single copy in one statement, so they cannot disagree, and no report pays the extra join.

choices.text: He is right: without it, a rename would rewrite 375,294 rows, nearly half of the warehouse's biggest table.
choices.why: 375,294 is the one big table's count. In the star the rename writes 1,185 rows of a small dimension, which the load does without noticing.

choices.text: Repetition is free in a column store, where the star and the wide table take exactly the same bytes.
choices.why: Lesson 6 measured the wide table at 1.3 times the star by column: cheap, not free. And the argument for 3NF is about writers, not bytes.

prompt: In the shop's database a customer who moves is one `UPDATE` of one row, which is what third normal form buys. A colleague wants `dim_customer` loaded the same way each month, overwriting city and state, so that the warehouse also keeps each fact in one place. What happens to the manager's report of 2024 sales by state?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 2; Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 5.

choices.text: It changes after each load, as everyone who moved since takes their 2024 sales to the new state.
choices.why: Right. That is type 1: asked in October and again in December, lesson 5's 2024 figure for Minas Gerais differed by R$ 9,392.24.

choices.text: The report stays put, since each sale line stores the buyer's state, as each order line stores its price.
choices.why: The till copied the price into every line and copied no state. A sale reaches the state through the customer, so it gets whatever the dimension says now.

choices.text: A customer who moved has each sale counted twice, once in each state.
choices.why: Double counting comes from type 2 versions that overlap. An overwrite leaves one row per customer, holding only the new state.

choices.text: During the load a customer holds two states at once, and a report run mid-load sees both.
choices.why: The load runs inside a transaction, so a reader sees the old dimension or the new one. The damage is in what the new one says about the past.

prompt: On a PostgreSQL copy of the star, the monthly dashboard sums `net_cents` over every sale since January 2024, grouped by month and department, and it is slow. A colleague runs `CREATE INDEX ON fact_sales (date_key)`, since every report filters on the date. What happens, and what does the warehouse course offer instead?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 9; Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 6.

choices.text: The plan switches to an index scan, and just the dashboard's months are read from the table.
choices.why: The dashboard asks for every month there is. An index pays when it rules out most of the table, and this filter rules out nothing.

choices.text: The new index waits for `ANALYZE`; with fresh statistics the planner picks it.
choices.why: Fresh statistics would only confirm what the planner already knows: the query wants every row, and reading the table straight through is cheaper.

choices.text: It still reads the whole table, rightly; a 616-row aggregate is the tool.
choices.why: Right. The query summarises all of the table, so no index can skip any of it. Summing once at load time and reading 616 rows can.

choices.text: With `INCLUDE (net_cents)` the index covers the query, and the table itself is skipped.
choices.why: It would not even cover it, since the department comes through `book_key`. And a query over most of the table wants the table, not an index.

prompt: The SQL course batches a ten-million-row backfill into commits of a few thousand rows, while the warehouse wraps each whole load in one transaction. Asked why one team does opposite things, which answer holds?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 8; Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 6.

choices.text: A warehouse load works without row locks, so a long transaction there is free.
choices.why: Any transaction keeps the rows it wrote locked until it ends. What makes a long one acceptable here is that nobody else is writing the warehouse.

choices.text: Batching is about speed, since one large commit writes more slowly than many small ones.
choices.why: Lesson 8 batches for the locks, the dead row versions and the ability to stop, and says plainly that it gives up atomicity to get them.

choices.text: The backfill is safe to rerun while the load is not, which is why the load alone gets one.
choices.why: Lesson 8 had to make the backfill resumable precisely because it gave up the transaction. Being rerunnable is not what separates the two.

choices.text: The tills write beside the backfill; the warehouse has one writer, and a report must never see half a load.
choices.why: Right. On the shop's database a long transaction blocks the tills and holds dead versions. In the warehouse, all or nothing costs only the load's own time.

prompt: Order 112406 has three lines worth 3,290, 2,990 and 6,890 centavos, and paid R$ 14.90 of shipping. Suppose it had been paid with a gift card and a card: two payments that together cover everything it owed. Joined row to row with `fact_payments` on `order_id`, as in lesson 4's fan-out query, what does `sum(p.amount_cents)` come to for this order?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 5; Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 4.

prompt: So as not to recompute two years every night, as `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` would, the team keeps `agg_sales_month` as a table that the load updates for the current month only. Then lesson 6's correction lands: one line of order 112406, sold in 2024, is R$ 10.00 lower in `fact_sales`. What stops the dashboard from showing the old figure?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 7; Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 6.

choices.text: `REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY`, which works out which rows have changed and recomputes just the months involved.
choices.why: The summary is no longer a materialised view, and `CONCURRENTLY` still reruns the whole query; it only lets readers carry on while it does.

choices.text: A step at the end of the load that compares the summary's total with the fact table's and fails on a gap.
choices.why: Right. The table never rewrites a month it is not loading, so only a check can turn the ten-real gap into an error somebody sees.

choices.text: The summary is safe as it is: built from `fact_sales`, it agrees with it by construction.
choices.why: A derived table is as old as its last rebuild. Lesson 6 showed the two totals 1,000 centavos apart after exactly this correction.

choices.text: Replacing the table with a plain view, current at each read and as quick to read.
choices.why: A view stores nothing, so it is current, but every read runs the aggregation over all of `fact_sales` again.

prompt: Finance wants a page showing the receipts taken so far today and, under it, the same total split by payment method. The two queries must agree to the centavo while the tills keep selling. Where does the page run, and how?
hint: Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 1; Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 8.

choices.text: On the warehouse, which is built for totals and keeps reports away from the tills.
choices.why: The warehouse is as fresh as last night's load, so at three in the afternoon it knows nothing about today's receipts.

choices.text: On the shop's database at the default `READ COMMITTED`, which hides uncommitted work.
choices.why: Each statement takes its own view, so a sale committed between the two queries lands in one total and not in the other.

choices.text: On the shop's own database, with both statements in one transaction at `REPEATABLE READ`.
choices.why: Right. A question about now belongs on the operational side, and one view for the whole transaction makes the two totals agree.

choices.text: On a read replica at `READ UNCOMMITTED`, so that the page does not wait for a till.
choices.why: PostgreSQL runs that level as `READ COMMITTED`: two statements, two views, and the totals can still differ.

prompt: The star answered revenue by department and tier through three joins in 0.021 seconds; the wide table, with none, took 0.017. A teammate still wants every report moved to the wide table because joins are slow. In the plan vocabulary of the SQL course, what were those three joins?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 10; Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 6.

choices.text: Nested Loops, each fact row looking up its dimension row through an index on the key.
choices.why: That is close to 900 thousand lookups per dimension. A Nested Loop suits a small outer side, and here the outer side is the whole fact table.

choices.text: Merge Joins, because the fact table is already sorted on each of its keys.
choices.why: `fact_sales` is stored in order of order number, so it is not sorted on `book_key` or `customer_key`.

choices.text: Nested Loops with a sequential scan inside, the shape that means an index is missing.
choices.why: That shape reads a dimension once per fact row and would have taken far longer than 21 milliseconds.

choices.text: Hash Joins: each small dimension hashed in memory, and the fact table streamed past once.
choices.why: Right. Hashing a few thousand rows costs a fraction of a millisecond, which is why the two timings sit inside the noise.

prompt: Ana builds her first star from the shop's operational schema. Which of that schema's habits does lesson 2's star deliberately leave behind? Choose all that apply.
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 7; Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 2.

choices.text: A book's format kept as a code that a lookup table translates
choices.why: Left behind: `dim_book` says `hardcover`, because a code that needs a lookup is a join every report must remember.

choices.text: Money held as an integer number of cents rather than as a float
choices.why: Kept: `fact_sales` stays in integer cents, and its 887,477 lines add up to the exact centavo.

choices.text: The category tree as a table that points at itself, walked with `WITH RECURSIVE` by each report
choices.why: Left behind: the load flattens the ragged tree once, and every book row carries all three levels.

choices.text: Cancelled orders kept in the table, for each query to filter out
choices.why: Left behind: `fact_sales` drops them once, in its `WHERE`, so no report can forget.

prompt: After an `UPDATE`, both PostgreSQL and a Delta table keep the old version of the row for a while, and both clean up with a command called vacuum. What decides how long the old version can survive in each?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 8; Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 10.

choices.text: In both, the oldest reader still running, since vacuum leaves alone any version somebody may read.
choices.why: True of PostgreSQL only. Delta's vacuum goes by a retention period, and lesson 10's dry run with zero retention picked a file that versions 0 and 1 still needed.

choices.text: In PostgreSQL, the `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` setting; in Delta, the log's next checkpoint.
choices.why: The timeout ends idle sessions, which helps vacuum, but it sets no retention. A checkpoint summarises the log and deletes no data file.

choices.text: In both, the next compaction, which rewrites each page or file and drops what is old.
choices.why: PostgreSQL's vacuum reclaims dead versions without rewriting the table, and Delta's deletes files by age, not by compaction.

choices.text: In PostgreSQL, the oldest open transaction; in Delta, a retention period, seven days by default.
choices.why: Right. PostgreSQL keeps what a running transaction may still need; Delta keeps old files for a window, and time travel works only inside it.

prompt: The manager says the revenue-by-month dashboard on the warehouse is too slow. Put the architect's steps in the order the two courses ask for them, first step first.
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 7; Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 6.
items: Read the dashboard query's plan and find where the time goes
Fix what the plan shows, such as a missing index or a function around a column
If it is still too slow for the people waiting, build a monthly aggregate from the fact table
Rebuild the aggregate in the nightly load, in the same transaction as the facts
End the load by comparing the aggregate's total with the fact table's
trap: The tempting order starts by building the aggregate, because the dashboard is what is slow. Both courses put measuring first: a summary over a query that only lacked an index is a nightly job and a staleness window bought for nothing.

prompt: A catalogue page lists 40 publishers, each with all of its books, a few hundred per publisher, and every publisher row carries a long description. `pg_stat_statements` shows the books query called 40 times for each page. Which fix does lesson 11 point to?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 11.

choices.text: One `LEFT JOIN` of publishers to books, so that the whole page comes back in a single statement.
choices.why: It repeats each publisher's long description on every one of its books, hundreds of copies. The join suits a to-one relationship.

choices.text: Load the publishers, then the books of all of them in one more statement, by their set of ids.
choices.why: Right. Two statements per page whatever the number of publishers, and each book comes back once.

choices.text: Mark the books relationship as eager on the publisher model, which fixes the problem on each screen.
choices.why: It also loads the books on every screen that fetches a publisher, including those that show only a name. The instruction belongs where the loop starts.

choices.text: Cache each publisher's books, as each of the 40 queries takes a fraction of a millisecond.
choices.why: The cost is the count of round trips, and lesson 11 says the fix is never caching, denormalising or a bigger server.

prompt: The order history screen runs `SELECT id, placed_at, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 20`. Which index lets PostgreSQL go straight to the customer, read twenty entries and stop?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 9.

choices.text: One index on `(customer_id)` and another on `(placed_at)`
choices.why: Neither alone gives one customer's orders in date order, so the database fetches them all, sorts them and keeps twenty.

choices.text: `(customer_id) INCLUDE (placed_at)`
choices.why: `INCLUDE` stores the date without sorting by it, so the customer's entries come out in no date order and still need a sort.

choices.text: `(customer_id, placed_at)`
choices.why: Right. Equality first, then the sort column: the customer's entries sit together in date order, and reading them backwards is free.

choices.text: `(placed_at, customer_id)` by itself
choices.why: Sorted by date first, one customer's orders are scattered across the whole index, and the leftmost-prefix rule gives a filter on `customer_id` nothing.

prompt: An events table inserts three million rows a day and deletes them again, never holding more than a few million at once. Its key is `integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`. With lesson 3's range for `integer`, about how many years until the ids run out? Round to the nearest whole year.
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 3.

prompt: Three copies of an application behind a load balancer cannot share one SQLite file. On a single machine, WAL mode lets readers carry on beside the one ___ that SQLite allows for the whole file at a time.
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 12.

prompt: At two in the afternoon an application on Oracle hangs, waiting on a lock on one customer's row. The DBA finds the lock held by an analyst who ran an `UPDATE` in SQL\*Plus before lunch. Why is it still held?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 13.

choices.text: The server has no autocommit and SQL\*Plus sent no commit, so the transaction is open.
choices.why: Right. Row locks last until `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`, and nobody has typed either.

choices.text: Oracle runs at `SERIALIZABLE` by default, a level that holds each lock it takes for an hour.
choices.why: Oracle's default is `READ COMMITTED`, and no level holds a lock for a set time; it lasts until the transaction ends.

choices.text: The `UPDATE` became a deadlock, which Oracle waits on until somebody notices.
choices.why: Oracle detects deadlocks and rolls one side back with `ORA-00060`. Here one session simply holds a lock.

choices.text: The undo ran out, and the row stays locked until `ORA-01555` frees it.
choices.why: `ORA-01555` refuses a long query whose undo was recycled. It neither takes locks nor frees them.

prompt: Match each situation to what lesson 8 reaches for first.
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 8.

pairs.left: A screen that saves one order and reads nothing twice
A reconciliation whose three queries must see the same data
A withdrawal allowed only while the account's rows still sum above zero
Two sign-ups racing for the same username

prompt: On PostgreSQL, `SELECT customer_id, sum(total) AS spent FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING spent > 1000` is refused, and the error says the column does not exist. Why?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 4.

choices.text: That clause runs before `SELECT`, so the name `spent` has not been given yet.
choices.why: Right. `HAVING` runs before `SELECT`, and of the clauses only `ORDER BY` runs after it, so that is the one that can use the alias.

choices.text: An aggregate is not allowed in `HAVING`, so the total has to be filtered in `WHERE`.
choices.why: The other way round: `WHERE` runs before the groups exist and cannot see a sum. A condition on a sum belongs in `HAVING`.

choices.text: The alias needs double quotes, because PostgreSQL folds names written without them.
choices.why: `spent` is already lower case, and quoting it changes nothing: the name does not exist yet when `HAVING` runs.

choices.text: `GROUP BY` threw `total` away, so the comparison has lost its column.
choices.why: The sum is computed from `total` in each group. What is missing is only the name, which `SELECT` gives later.

prompt: Lesson 7 imagines seven nodes with one shop each, and by its skew query the website's node would hold 378,374 of the 887,477 sale lines. What is the ratio lesson 7 says to watch, the fullest node against the average, to two decimal places?
hint: Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 7.

hint: Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 10.
