hint: Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 4.

pairs.left: An order's shipping fee copied onto each of its lines
pairs.right: a share of the fee per line, in proportion to its value

pairs.left: Revenue by author counting a three-author book three times
pairs.right: a weight on each row of the bridge table

pairs.left: Walk-in sales whose customer is empty
A receipt's lines to be grouped, with nothing more to say about the receipt

prompt: A library chain's warehouse records, per branch and month, the loans made, the fines collected, the books on the shelves at month-end and the share of loans returned late. Which of these may a report add up across the twelve months of a year? Choose all that apply.
hint: Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 2.

choices.text: The books on the shelves at month-end
choices.why: A level, like `on_hand`: twelve counts of mostly the same copies, which add up to no number of books.

choices.text: The loans made
choices.why: A flow: each loan happened in one month, so the months add up to the year's loans.

choices.text: The fines collected
choices.why: Money taken during the month is a flow, and flows add over time.

choices.text: The share of loans returned late
choices.why: A ratio. Store the late loans and all loans, sum each, and divide last.

prompt: A distributor's sales force has managers who can sit any number of levels above a seller, and reports ask for everything sold under a given manager. How does lesson 3 model that hierarchy?
hint: Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 3.

choices.text: Flatten it into fixed level columns, repeating the level below wherever one is missing.
choices.why: That suits the shop's three levels because the depth has a maximum. Here no number of columns is enough.

choices.text: Snowflake each level into its own table, joined in a chain from seller to the top.
choices.why: The chain needs one join per level, and with no fixed depth no query knows how many to write.

choices.text: A hierarchy bridge, with one row for each ancestor and descendant pair and the distance between them.
choices.why: Right. Everything under a manager is then one join, at any depth.

choices.text: A junk dimension holding each combination of manager and seller that occurs.
choices.why: A junk dimension collects small flags of an event. It knows nothing about who sits above whom.

prompt: Most dashboard queries on `fact_sales` filter on one shop, and the Parquet file is written in order of order number. What does writing it sorted by shop and date change?
hint: Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 8.

choices.text: A shop's rows sit together, so the zone maps let a shop filter skip most row groups.
choices.why: Right. Zone maps prune only when the rows a query wants sit together, and `shop_key` also falls to 524 bytes, seven runs.

choices.text: The file shrinks to a fraction of its size, since each column now compresses as runs.
choices.why: The total barely moved, 9,331,332 against 9,317,594 bytes. One column shrank enormously and `date_key` grew.

choices.text: A query does the same work, since row groups keep statistics for `date_key` alone.
choices.why: Every row group records a minimum and maximum for every column, `shop_key` included.

choices.text: Each shop gets a file of its own, so a filter on one shop opens one file of seven.
choices.why: That is partitioning, which splits files by folder. Sorting keeps one file and orders the rows inside it.

prompt: On Snowflake, the month-end load makes the finance dashboards wait, and nobody can say how many credits each team uses. Which of lesson 9's habits answers both?
hint: Data Modelling and the Data Warehouse, lesson 9.

choices.text: One larger warehouse for everybody, so that the load finishes sooner and frees the dashboards.
choices.why: A bigger shared warehouse still mixes the two workloads and still sends one bill for both teams.

choices.text: Clustering the fact table by date, so that each query reads fewer bytes.
choices.why: Clustering cuts the work of a query. It neither keeps one workload from waiting on another nor splits the bill.

choices.text: Auto-suspend after a minute of idleness, so that idle hours stop costing credits.
choices.why: It saves the idle hours, but the load and the dashboards still queue on one warehouse.

choices.text: Separate warehouses for separate workloads, each on its own credits.
choices.why: Right. The load cannot slow dashboards that run on their own warehouse, and each team's consumption shows on its own.

prompt: Regina wants the Portal B2B to promise the bakeries 99.5% for the stock check in their basket, measured each month. Rui's team offers an operational level agreement of 99.5% for the bus, and SAP measures 99.0% outside its planned window. What should Joana answer before anyone signs?
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 12; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 8.

choices.text: With the portal's 99.9%, the three multiply to about 98.4%: offer less, or take SAP out of the wait.
choices.why: Right: every synchronous part is a factor, and the agreements underneath have to reach the promise before it is signed. SAP's 1% is most of the gap.

choices.text: Sign it: the bus's agreement already matches the target, and a chain is as available as its best-covered link.
choices.why: A chain is less available than its weakest member: 0.999 × 0.995 × 0.99 is 98.41%, below every one of the three.

choices.text: Sign once SAP's team turns its 99.0% into an underpinning contract, so that a credit pays the bakeries for any miss.
choices.why: SAP's team is part of the same company, so its commitment would be an OLA, and a credit leaves the chain at about 98.4%.

choices.text: Promise 99.5% over a year instead of a month: the same figure, and easier for the chain.
choices.why: The same percentage over another window is another promise, and the chain misses 99.5% over a year as well.

prompt: In October 2026 Joana counts 23 change requests waiting for Rui's integration team, and the average request waits 9 weeks before anybody starts it. Treat the waiting line as a stable system and apply Little's law. About how many requests a week does the team take off the line? Give two decimal places.
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 8; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 3.

prompt: Every change to any integration at Serra Alta waits for Rui's team of four, the only people who know the bus. In the scaling lesson's terms, which arrangement does the plan for shrinking the bus move towards?
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 8; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 5.

choices.text: Rui's team becomes a feature team, taking every integration change from request to production on its own.
choices.why: That is roughly what it does today, and the queue is the result: the people who know what a change should do cannot make it.

choices.text: The teams at each end own their translations, and Rui's team runs the platform for them as an internal supplier.
choices.why: Right: a transformation moves to the team that owns its format, and a platform every team builds on can stay with one component team that serves the others.

choices.text: Rui's team is dissolved into the other teams, since LeSS requires feature teams and leaves no component team.
choices.why: The bus lesson keeps 24 routing flows and a team that runs MQ, and the scaling lesson lets a platform stay with one team.

choices.text: Each of the other teams gets one of Rui's four people, so that a bus specialist sits inside every team that asks.
choices.why: Four people cannot sit in twelve teams. Specialists end up working across teams, and the plan moves the transformations instead.

prompt: The portal team usually deploys several small changes a week. During the freeze that ends on 10 November it holds eight changes back, and plans to put all eight into production in one deployment on the 11th. By both lessons, what is wrong with that plan?
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 12; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 13.

choices.text: Nothing: a freeze is a period without risk, so whatever waited through it is safe once it ends.
choices.why: A freeze moves changes to the weeks either side of it. Waiting tested nothing, and the risk arrives with the queue.

choices.text: The 11th is still frozen: the freeze runs through the close and the payment to the 26th of November.
choices.why: The freeze ends on the evening of the 10th; the 11th to the 26th are the eleven working days open for changes.

choices.text: The freeze has piled the risk into one batch; ship the eight as small deploys across the days that are open.
choices.why: Right: a freeze moves changes to the week after it, and small changes are easier to test, understand and undo, which is why frequent deploys also fail less.

choices.text: It lowers deployment frequency, which DORA's research treats as the price paid for a lower change failure rate.
choices.why: The research found the opposite: the throughput pair and the stability pair do not trade off, and the teams that deploy most often fail least.

prompt: Serra Alta's cutover runbook budgets nine hours from the freeze to the go/no-go decision and keeps three hours in reserve before the 08:00 deadline. A colleague proposes adding 20% to each step's own time instead, and dropping the separate reserve. What do both lessons say?
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 14; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 11.

choices.text: Accept it: a margin on every step is the contingency reserve that the risk lesson builds from the register.
choices.why: The contingency reserve is held centrally and not spread across tasks, because a reserve divided among tasks is spent by them.

choices.text: Accept it, and decide at 10:00 when the window closes, since every step now carries a margin of its own.
choices.why: The rehearsed rollback takes about two hours, so a decision after 08:00 could not be undone inside the window.

choices.text: Drop both margins: the second dress rehearsal took 5 h 50 min, which leaves the night hours to spare.
choices.why: One rehearsal measured one night. The runbook keeps its reserve for what the real night does differently, and keeps it in one place.

choices.text: Keep a single buffer ahead of go/no-go: margins spread over steps get spent, and 08:00 is the window minus the rollback.
choices.why: Right: a reserve held in one place is spent only when something happens, like the critical chain's single buffer, and the latest decision comes from the measured rollback.

prompt: For three weeks, customer service has logged calls from one supermarket chain whose orders never reached SAP, and closed each call by keying the order in by hand. Rui then finds those orders in the flow's dead-letter queue, all refused for a ship-to code SAP does not know. What was missing, by both lessons?
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 10; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 8.

choices.text: A problem record for the common cause, and an owner and an alarm on that flow's dead-letter queue.
choices.why: Right: each call was an incident and was restored, but one cause behind all of them is a problem, and a dead-letter queue nobody watches turns a loud failure into a silent one.

choices.text: Nothing: every incident was resolved, and restoring the service quickly is what incident management is for.
choices.why: Restoring each call was right. With the same cause behind every call, though, somebody had to investigate it, and nobody did.

choices.text: More retries on the flow, with backoff, so that each order reaches SAP once the code turns up there.
choices.why: An unknown code is a permanent failure: the hundredth try fails like the first, so retrying only delays the dead letter.

choices.text: Priority 1 for each of the calls, so that the help desk works on every one of them within fifteen minutes.
choices.why: Priority comes from impact and urgency, and restoring each call faster still leaves the cause unexamined.

prompt: Comparing the three ways to replace Coleta's payment, Marcos reads twice the row that sets each option against Sebastião's retirement at the end of June 2028. In the prioritisation lesson's urgency profiles, what is that row describing?
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 15; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 12.

choices.text: A standard cost, lost a little every month, so the totals on the sheet already price it and the row adds nothing.
choices.why: The sheet prices money paid. What Sebastião knows is not lost a little at a time; it goes on the day he leaves.

choices.text: A fixed-date cost: nothing is lost while he is there and much after, and B needs Coleta past it.
choices.why: Right: the parallel run is when differences appear, and B still needs Coleta, and so him, a month after he has gone.

choices.text: An intangible cost, small now and larger later, so the choice can wait until the parallel run shows a difference.
choices.why: Waiting for the parallel run is the problem: it is when differences appear, and an option that ends after June has nobody to explain them.

choices.text: An urgent cost, lost fast from day one, so the option that spends soonest goes first.
choices.why: Nothing is lost today while Sebastião is in the building. The loss begins on one date, which is the fixed-date shape.

prompt: A migration like Serra Alta's runs as a PRINCE2 project, with a time tolerance of one week on its cutover stage. Two weeks before the night, the last dress rehearsal overruns its time budget, and the rule written before the rehearsals says: a third rehearsal, and the cutover one month later. Which steps fit both lessons? Choose all that apply.
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 14; Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 7.

choices.text: Keep the date and let the go/no-go meeting decide on the night whether the overrun matters.
choices.why: Criteria written on the night are criteria bent on the night. At 05:00 the meeting only checks whether each written line is true.

choices.text: The project manager raises an exception to the board now, because the forecast already breaks the tolerance.
choices.why: An exception is raised on a forecast, not on an event, and a month's slip is far past a one-week time tolerance.

choices.text: A third rehearsal comes first, and the cutover moves to after the next payment, as the written rule says.
choices.why: The plan is ready when a rehearsal fits its budget and finds nothing new; a no is the plan working, not a failure.

choices.text: The project manager waits for the cutover weekend and tells the board only if the night itself overruns.
choices.why: PRINCE2 escalates when a forecast says a tolerance will be exceeded. Waiting for the event leaves the board nothing to decide.

prompt: Match each need on a new Serra Alta flow to the transformation pattern that meets it.
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 11.

pairs.left: A plant's 6 MB inspection report should not travel through every hop and every log of the flow
Truck readings carry the driver's CPF, and the plant dashboard needs only the plant and the litres
Payments arrive as EDI, as JSON and as Salesforce records, and the ledger should read one format
A collection message carries only the farm code, and the receiver also needs the farm's route

prompt: The flow that feeds Salesforce from the `invoice.paid` topic is stopped for a deployment and stays down for ten minutes. Its subscription was created without the durable option. What happens to the payments published in those ten minutes?
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 10.

choices.text: They wait on the topic, and the flow reads them in order as soon as it reconnects, as it would from a queue.
choices.why: Only a durable subscription keeps the copies for a subscriber that is down and hands them over when it comes back.

choices.text: They go to the dead-letter queue, and somebody can replay them to Salesforce once the flow is running again.
choices.why: Nothing failed in a consumer. A subscription that is not durable has nobody to deliver to, so no copy is kept anywhere.

choices.text: That flow loses them: a subscription of that kind gets only what arrives while it is connected.
choices.why: Right: the difference is one word in the code, and ten minutes of restart quietly cost every payment made in them.

choices.text: The ledger and IBM BPM take them instead, because the three subscribers of a topic compete for each message.
choices.why: On a topic each subscriber gets a copy of its own. The other two get theirs, and Salesforce's copy has nowhere to go.

prompt: Configuration and extensions beside an ERP survive its upgrades; modifications inside it are broken by every one. SAP's name for keeping the inside free of modifications is a ___ core.
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 1.

prompt: Put these moments of option A, the SaaS product, in the order they happen within the 36 months of the sheet.
hint: Enterprise Software and Integration, lesson 15.
items: Serra Alta starts paying the subscription for 1,900 farms
The partner's implementation, parallel run included, comes to an end
The product pays its first farms, on 10 October 2027
Coleta is switched off, after the product's third payment
The price per farm rises to R$ 26 at the first renewal
trap: The tempting order starts the subscription when the product first pays a farm, as if paying began when the product works. Vendors start the clock at signature, so nine months are paid first.

prompt: A team's product owner answers the developers' questions once a week, at a fixed meeting. Few teams have XP's customer on site literally. What does the lesson say the principle survives as?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 4.

choices.text: A rule that the customer estimates each story, because the customer knows best what the work involves.
choices.why: In the planning game the developers estimate what a story costs; the customer decides value and order.

choices.text: A weekly review with the customer, which is what XP meant by putting the customer on site.
choices.why: XP wanted somebody answering the same day. A weekly meeting leaves developers guessing for days at a time.

choices.text: A place for the product owner at every Daily Scrum, however long the team then waits for decisions.
choices.why: The lesson measures the wait for an answer, not who attends which event.

choices.text: A test of how long a developer waits for an answer: hours is healthy, weeks is not.
choices.why: Right: the measure is the wait, and a team that waits weeks ends up building what it guessed.

prompt: A team scores four items on SAFe's three components of cost of delay and on job size, all on the modified Fibonacci scale. Put them in WSJF order, first to last.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 12.
items: Certificate renewal: value 2, time criticality 13, risk reduction 8; size 3
Clinic dashboard: value 5, time criticality 2, risk reduction 1; size 2
Pix at booking: value 13, time criticality 5, risk reduction 2; size 8
Patient history export: value 8, time criticality 2, risk reduction 1; size 8
trap: Ordering by user value puts Pix first and the certificate renewal last. WSJF adds time criticality and risk reduction to the value and divides by size: 23 ÷ 3, 8 ÷ 2, 20 ÷ 8 and 11 ÷ 8.

prompt: A project has a budget at completion of R$ 400,000 and planned to have R$ 160,000 of work finished by week 8. At week 8, 30% of its work is done, and it has spent R$ 130,000. What is its schedule performance index? Give two decimal places.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 6.

prompt: To report in hours, a department declares that one story point equals six hours. A 5-point story then takes 40 hours. By the lesson, what has the conversion done?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 10.

choices.text: Turned points into time estimates with an extra step, and made that story one somebody now has to explain.
choices.why: Right: a fixed rate brings back every weakness relative sizing was meant to avoid, and adds a hidden target per story.

choices.text: Made the department's teams comparable at last, because every one of their points now stands for the same six hours.
choices.why: Each team's points stay calibrated against its own reference stories; a rate on top changes the label and nothing else.

choices.text: Nothing harmful, provided the six hours were measured from the team's own past Sprints.
choices.why: The lesson objects to the fixed rate itself. If an organisation needs time, it should ask for estimates in time, openly.

choices.text: Given the department the use of velocity the lesson recommends: a forecast in hours for every story.
choices.why: The one legitimate use is a team forecasting its own future from its own past, in its own units.

prompt: A director asks for the team's delivery dashboard to be emailed to him at 08:00 every Monday, before the team's own review at 10:00, so that he can raise questions early. Which of the lesson's rules does that break?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 13.

choices.text: Team-level only: nobody's name may appear on a chart, and a director's copy would show the members.
choices.why: The dashboard stays a team-level one and names no person, so that rule still holds.

choices.text: The team sees them first: numbers that reach management before the team has looked become a report card.
choices.why: Right: the order in which people see the numbers is what turns a team's tool into a report card on the team.

choices.text: Trends, not targets: a director who reads a chart every week has set a target for each measure on it.
choices.why: Reading a chart sets no target. What this request changes is who looks at the numbers first.

choices.text: Never in a performance review: a Monday email to a director is where every appraisal starts.
choices.why: Nothing here touches anybody's review. The problem is the order in which the numbers are seen.

prompt: A team is cleaning up its risk register. By the PMBOK definition the lesson adopts, which of these entries are risks rather than issues? Choose all that apply.
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 11.

choices.text: The SMS gateway might raise its price when the contract comes up for renewal next year.
choices.why: It may or may not happen, and it would affect cost: an uncertain event, which is what a risk is.

choices.text: The hosting provider has announced that the current database version loses support on 31 August.
choices.why: Announced, with a date: it will happen, so it is an issue, and it goes into the backlog as work.

choices.text: An open-source PDF library might already produce the clinics' invoices, which would save a week.
choices.why: A risk can be good news. An uncertain event with a positive effect is an opportunity, and it belongs on the register.

choices.text: The only developer who knows the billing module has handed in her notice, and her last day is Friday.
choices.why: Nothing about it is uncertain any more. It needs a task and a deadline, not a probability.

prompt: For a new reporting module, an estimate by analogy says 12 working days, and a parametric estimate from the team's rate per report says 28. The sponsor suggests quoting the average, 20 days. What does the lesson say to do next?
hint: Management, Process and Estimation, lesson 9.

choices.text: Quote 20 days at 85% confidence, since two methods averaged make a stronger estimate than either alone.
choices.why: Agreement between independent methods is strong evidence. A disagreement means one of them rests on a wrong assumption, and an average hides which.

choices.text: Quote 28 days: estimates go wrong mostly on the short side, so the larger is safer.
choices.why: Taking the larger number still leaves the gap unexplained, and the gap is what the team has to look into.

choices.text: Find out which assumption differs between the methods: the disagreement is itself the finding.
choices.why: Right: when independent methods disagree, the next step is the assumption that differs, not the arithmetic between them.

choices.text: Quote 12 to 28 days as the range, since a good estimate is a range and this one contains both methods.
choices.why: A range is the right form, but this one is the width of a disagreement nobody has explained yet.
